title: NASA Urges Earthlings to Wave as Voyager 1 Hits One Light‑Day Distance – The Register
body:
The interstellar probe Voyager 1 is set to become the first human‑made object to travel a full light‑day away from Earth, a milestone that NASA is marking with a public “wave” of flashing lights on 17 November. The 45‑year‑old spacecraft will be roughly 25.9 billion kilometres (about 171 AU) from our planet, a distance that light covers in 24 hours. To celebrate, the agency has invited anyone with a flashlight, car headlights or any visible light source to flash a short burst of Morse code—“VGR” for Voyager 1—into the night sky, creating a symbolic salute for the lone voyager that has been journeying through interstellar space since 2012.

Voyager 1 was launched on 5 September 1977 as part of NASA’s twin‑probe mission to study the outer planets. After spectacular fly‑bys of Jupiter and Saturn, the spacecraft was redirected toward the heliopause, the outer boundary of the Sun’s magnetic bubble. In August 2012 it crossed that threshold, becoming the first human artifact to enter interstellar space. Since then, it has continued to send back data on cosmic rays, magnetic fields and plasma density, offering a unique glimpse of the environment beyond the solar system. The probe is powered by radioisotope thermoelectric generators that have been gradually losing output; by the time it reaches a light‑day distance its power will be just enough to keep its transmitter and a few essential systems operational for a few more years.

The “light‑day flash” campaign is a public outreach effort designed to connect people worldwide with a mission that otherwise feels abstract and distant. NASA will broadcast a brief audio cue on its social media channels, indicating the exact moment to emit the Morse‑code signal. Participants are asked to point a light source toward the sky for a few seconds, flashing the pattern “dot‑dash‑dot” (V), “dash‑dash‑dash” (G) and “dot‑dash‑dot” (R). While the signal will not be detected by the probe—its antenna is oriented away from Earth and the light will be far too faint to travel the immense distance—the gesture serves as a collective acknowledgment of humanity’s first step beyond the Sun’s immediate sphere of influence.

Experts note that the event underscores both the triumphs and the limitations of deep‑space exploration. Dr. Ellen Stofan, former NASA chief scientist, remarked that Voyager’s longevity is a testament to the engineering foresight of the 1970s, yet the mission also highlights how dependent we remain on a handful of aging spacecraft for data from beyond the heliosphere. “Voyager 1 is a time capsule of the era that launched it,” she said. “When it finally powers down, we will lose the only direct, real‑time measurements we have of interstellar space until the next generation of probes arrives.” The light‑day milestone therefore serves as a reminder that the window for gathering new data from Voyager is narrowing, prompting NASA and international partners to accelerate plans for dedicated interstellar missions such as the proposed Interstellar Probe, which aims to travel to 1,000 AU within 50 years.

Public reaction to the flash campaign has been enthusiastic, with amateur astronomers, schools and even city officials coordinating synchronized light shows. In several U.S. states, highway departments have scheduled brief “wave” sequences on major interstates, while astronomy clubs in Europe and Asia are organizing rooftop gatherings. Social media platforms are already buzzing with photos of illuminated skylines and videos of coordinated flashes, illustrating how a scientific milestone can inspire global participation.

Looking ahead, Voyager 1’s approach to a light‑day distance is not just a symbolic marker but also a practical gauge of its remaining operational lifespan. Engineers estimate that the probe will retain enough power to transmit until roughly 2028, after which its signal will fade into silence. The light‑day flash thus stands as both a celebration and a farewell, urging the public to recognize the fleeting nature of our current interstellar reach. As humanity prepares for the next era of deep‑space exploration, the collective wave of lights serves as a poignant reminder that, even from a quarter of a light‑year away, our curiosity and sense of wonder remain firmly anchored to Earth.
